say.text: A patient has right iliac fossa (RIF) pain, and the examiner has three manoeuvres to choose from. See what you already hold.
Which one tests for the **psoas sign**?

choices.label: Rotate the flexed right hip inwards, patient supine
Press firmly over the left iliac fossa, patient supine
Extend the right hip, patient lying on the left
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which movement stretches the psoas, the muscle a retrocaecal appendix can lie on.
Tempting: both are right-hip manoeuvres, so they blur into one 'hip test' in memory.
But internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign, which suggests a pelvic appendix. The psoas sign is hip extension, with the patient on the left.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the movement before the name: extension is psoas, and inward rotation of the flexed hip is obturator.

say.text: Tempting: pressing the left side is one of the signs you have seen, so it feels like a hip test.
But pressure over the left fossa is Rovsing's sign, which causes pain in the right fossa. Psoas is hip extension.

sure_note.text: You were sure about a left-sided press. Rovsing's is the sign where the pressure and the pain sit on opposite sides.

say.text: Yes. Extending the right hip stretches the psoas, and a retrocaecal appendix can lie on that muscle.
Retrocaecal is the commonest position of the appendix, so this sign points to where the appendix most often lies.
Put the three side by side. Psoas: extend the right hip with the patient on the left. Pain means a retrocaecal appendix lying on the psoas.
Obturator: flex the right hip and rotate it inwards. Pain means a pelvic appendix in contact with obturator internus.
Rovsing: press the left iliac fossa and feel the right. Pressure and pain sit on opposite sides, and the exam loves mixing these three.
Now the direction, which is where most learners slip. Which statement about Rovsing's sign is correct?

choices.label: Pressure in the right iliac fossa causes pain in the left
Pressure in the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right fossa
Extending the right hip causes pain in the right iliac fossa

say.text: Yes. The sign crosses the abdomen: pressure on the left, pain on the right.
Device: press the side without the pain, and listen for the pain on the other side.
Tempting: you remember 'right-sided pain', so the pressure seems to belong where the pain is.
But the press goes on the left. Pressure in the right fossa is not Rovsing's sign. Predict the pain site from the press site.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so narrate the sign as: press here, hurts there. Press left, hurts right.

say.text: Tempting: extension is the psoas movement, so it feels like it belongs to Rovsing's statement too.
But the right-hip extension test is the psoas sign. Rovsing's is a left-sided press.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check each sign against its own manoeuvre: psoas is hip extension.

say.text: The examiner flexes the right hip and rotates the leg inwards. The patient winces with hypogastric pain.
Name the sign.

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with the movement: which one rotates the flexed hip? That movement is tested against one muscle in the pelvis.
Yes. Internal rotation of the flexed hip is the obturator sign.
Hypogastric pain on this movement points to a pelvic appendix in contact with obturator internus.
Tempting: both are right-hip manoeuvres, so psoas feels like the obvious name for any hip movement.
But the psoas sign is hip extension. Rotating the flexed hip inwards is the obturator sign.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the sign from the movement: rotation of the flexed hip is obturator, not psoas.

say.text: Tempting: Rovsing's is the sign you met first, so it comes to mind for any right-sided test.
But Rovsing's is pressure over the left fossa, not a hip movement. This movement is the obturator sign.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match the sign to its manoeuvre before its name: a hip movement is not Rovsing's.

say.text: A young man has loin pain that comes on with hip extension, and little tenderness in front.
Which pairing of sign and appendix position fits?

choices.label: Psoas with pelvic; obturator with retrocaecal
Psoas with retrocaecal; obturator with pelvic
Psoas with retrocaecal; rectal tenderness with retrocaecal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Pair each sign with the position it points to: which position lies on the psoas, and which lies on obturator internus?
Yes. A retrocaecal appendix lies on the psoas, so hip extension hurts. A pelvic one lies on obturator internus.
Loin pain with little anterior tenderness fits the retrocaecal position.
Tempting: psoas and obturator are both hip signs, so swapping their positions looks like a small slip.
But the psoas sign suggests a retrocaecal appendix, and the obturator sign suggests a pelvic one. Each sign follows its organ.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link each sign to the position it touches: a retrocaecal appendix lies on the psoas.

say.text: Tempting: the psoas half is right, so the second half feels right too. Rectal tenderness is easy to attach to the wrong site.
But right-sided rectal tenderness suggests a pelvic appendix touching the rectum. Loin pain with little anterior tenderness fits a retrocaecal one.

sure_note.text: You were sure about the psoas half, so check the rest of the pair separately: rectal tenderness goes with the pelvis.

say.text: Why does a pelvic appendix cause diarrhoea, frequency and right-sided rectal tenderness?

choices.label: It lies on the psoas muscle, stretching it
It lies against the rectum and bladder, irritating them
It lies behind the caecum, irritating the ureter

say.text: Yes. A pelvic appendix lies against the rectum and bladder, so it irritates them.
Right-sided rectal tenderness points the same way.
Tempting: the retrocaecal picture is the one you have been using, so it feels like it should explain every sign.
But lying on the psoas or behind the caecum describes a retrocaecal appendix. Pelvic symptoms come from the rectum and bladder it touches.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which organ the appendix touches before you attach a symptom to a position.

say.text: The Alvarado (MANTRELS) score is out of 10, and its items do not all carry the same weight.
Which two items score 2 points each?

choices.label: Tenderness in the right iliac fossa and rebound
Tenderness in the right iliac fossa and leucocytosis
Migration of pain to the right fossa and rebound tenderness
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about which items are the most specific: the appendix itself, and the body's response to it in the blood.
Yes. Tenderness in the RIF and leucocytosis are the two items weighted 2.
Every other item scores 1.
Tempting: migration and rebound are signs of peritoneal irritation, so they feel like the strong items.
But only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2. Migration and rebound each score 1.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so rebuild the score from the table, not from how strong a sign feels.

say.text: Tempting: you kept the right item, RIF tenderness, and rebound feels like its partner.
But rebound scores 1. The second 2-point item is leucocytosis.

sure_note.text: You were sure about the tenderness, but the second 2-point item is the blood count, not the rebound.

say.text: She has migration of pain, nausea, RIF tenderness, rebound tenderness and a raised total count. She is afebrile, has no anorexia, and the differential is not back yet.
What is her Alvarado total?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Score each item once. Only two items carry 2 points, so check which two before you add.
Yes. Migration 1, nausea 1, RIF tenderness 2, rebound 1, leucocytosis 2: the total is 7.
A total of 7 or more makes appendicitis likely. It raises the probability; it does not confirm the diagnosis.
Tempting: migration and rebound both feel strong, so they seem to earn 2 points each.
But only RIF tenderness and leucocytosis score 2. Scoring migration and rebound at 2 gives 9, not the total of 7.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count each item at its table weight, not at its feel.

say.text: Tempting: a raised count can look like a lab result that adds less to the story.
But leucocytosis is one of the two 2-point items. Scoring it at 1 gives 6; the correct total is 7.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the leucocytosis weight in the table: it scores 2.

say.text: A young woman has sudden mid-cycle right iliac fossa pain. There is no migration, she is afebrile and her count is normal. The pain settles over hours.
Most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about timing. When in the cycle does this pain start, and how fast does it settle?
Yes. Mittelschmerz is pain from a ruptured Graafian follicle, which gives sudden mid-cycle pain in a woman.
The settling course and normal count fit it. RIF pain in a woman has its own list, and appendicitis is only one item on it.
Tempting: RIF pain in a young woman looks like the textbook appendicitis picture, so the answer seems set.
But RIF pain does not always mean appendicitis. Women have their own differential, including mittelschmerz.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask first what else gives RIF pain in this group before you settle on appendicitis.

say.text: Tempting: pelvic inflammatory disease is a real cause of RIF pain in women.
But this stem gives one settling episode with a normal count, which fits a ruptured follicle better.

sure_note.text: You were sure about the pelvic option, so compare how each one fits this timeline.
